title: Opening: soðgied wrecan
short: 'I can tell a true song about myself': the first-person opening of a poem preserved only in the Exeter Book.
body: The Seafarer (124 lines) is in the Exeter Book (fols 81b-83a), after The Wanderer and other poems. 'Soðgied' is 'true tale, true song'; 'wrecan' is 'to utter, recite'. The opening resembles The Wife's Lament ('Ic þis giedd wrece / bi me ful geomorre') and Deor, and marks the poem as a personal account. 'Siþas secgan' ('tell my journeys') announces the subject. 'Geswincdagum' ('days of toil') and 'earfoðhwile' ('time of hardship') set the tone. Whether the voyages are literal, allegorical, or both, is the central critical question. Ezra Pound's 1911 version translated only to l. 99 and dropped the Christian ending.

title: nearo nihtwaco æt nacan stefnan
short: The anxious night-watch at the ship's prow while it beats along the cliffs.
body: 'Nearo' is 'narrow, anxious, perilous'. 'Nihtwaco' means 'night-watch'. 'Naca' is a poetic word for 'ship' and 'stefn' is 'prow' (modern 'stem'). 'Þonne he be clifum cnossað' ('when it knocks along the cliffs'): the ship pounds near the rocky coast. 'Atol yþa gewealc' ('the terrible rolling of waves') recurs at l. 46. The speaker's experience is concrete; the sea-voyage is described from inside.

title: Cold fetters and hot sorrow (ll. 8-12)
short: His feet were bound by frost in cold fetters, while cares sighed hot about his heart: a paradox of cold and heat.
body: 'Calde geþrungen' ('pinched by cold'), 'forste gebunden' ('bound by frost'), 'caldum clommum' ('in cold clamps'): the feet are as if chained. Against this, the cares 'seofedun hat ymb heortan' ('sighed hot about the heart'). 'Seofian' is 'to lament'. The contrast of outer cold and inner heat is a key image of the poem, also used of the mind in l. 64 ('hatran'). 'Hungor innan slat merewerges mod' ('hunger tore within the sea-weary mind'): 'merewerig' occurs only here. The alliteration on c and h reinforces the sensations.

title: A defective line
short: 'Deprived of dear kinsmen' stands as a short line of its own in the printed text; editors differ on whether anything is lost.
body: 'Winemæg' is 'dear kinsman' and 'bidroren' (from bedreosan) is 'deprived'. The manuscript is written continuously like prose, and editors print 'winemægum bidroren' as a short line with no matching half-line, so some suspect a loss in copying. The theme of loss of kin is the exile's condition, as in The Wanderer ('winemæga hryre', l. 7). Editions differ in how they set out the lines here; consult the apparatus of the edition in use.

title: The bird catalogue: swan, gannet, curlew, gull
short: Instead of hall-joy he takes his pleasure in the swan's song, the gannet's cry, the curlew's voice and the gull's singing.
body: The birds stand in place of the hall's music and company. 'Ylfete' is the (whooper) swan; 'ganet' is the gannet; 'huilpe' is probably the curlew; 'mæw' is the gull. Each cry is matched with a hall pleasure: 'to gomene' ('as entertainment'), 'fore hleahtor wera' ('instead of men's laughter'), 'fore medodrince' ('instead of mead-drinking'). This ironic substitution is like the hall dream in The Wanderer. Ornithologists and editors have discussed which species are meant. Ezra Pound's paraphrase made the passage famous.

title: stearn ... isigfeþera; earn ... urigfeþra
short: Storms beat the cliffs where the tern answered, icy-feathered; the eagle often screamed, dewy-feathered.
body: 'Stearn' is probably the tern and 'earn' the eagle. The compounds 'isigfeþera' ('icy-feathered') and 'urigfeþra' ('dewy- or wet-feathered') are near-rhymes and occur only here. The eagle 'bigeal' ('screamed about') is a reminder of the beasts of battle. 'Ne ænig hleomæga feasceaftig ferð frefran meahte' ('no protecting kinsman could comfort the destitute spirit'). Gordon prints the text with comment on the bird identifications.

title: wlonc ond wingal
short: 'Proud and flushed with wine': the comfortable town-dweller who cannot imagine the seafarer's pain.
body: 'Wlonc' is 'proud, splendid' (also 'arrogant'), and 'wingal' is 'wine-flushed, merry with wine'. The man who lives 'in burgum' ('in towns, fortified places') and has had little of 'bealosiþa' ('bitter journeys') cannot believe what the seafarer endured. The same alliterating pair appears in The Ruin (l. 34) of the vanished warriors in the bath-city. In Christian readings the contrast is between worldly comfort and spiritual exile, but it can also be read socially.

title: Nap nihtscua, norþan sniwde
short: The night-shadow darkened, it snowed from the north, frost bound the ground, hail fell on earth, 'coldest of grains'.
body: 'Nap' is the past tense of 'nipan' ('to grow dark'). The half-line matches The Wanderer l. 104, 'nipeð nihtscua'. 'Hrim hrusan bond' ('frost bound the earth') and 'corna caldast' ('coldest of grains', hail) use the binding image and a riddle-like kenning for hail. The repeated use of 'Forþon' at l. 33 follows, a turning point in the poem. The seasonal sequence then reverses into spring at l. 48.

title: Forþon: the problem word
short: 'Forþon' can mean 'therefore', 'because' or 'indeed'; its many uses make the poem's logic hard to follow.
body: 'Forþon' (also 'forðon') usually means 'therefore' or 'because'. In The Seafarer it occurs six times in the first 72 lines (ll. 27, 33, 39, 58, 64, 72) and twice more in the close (ll. 103, 108), often at key turns, notably here at l. 33. The thoughts of his heart urge him to try the high streams himself, though he has just described the sea's misery. Many editors take some uses as 'indeed' or 'and yet' or as a simple connector. The logic depends on how one reads the speaker's attitude to the sea. Gordon and Klinck discuss the problem; Mitchell's syntax work treats the word in detail.

title: elþeodigra eard: peregrinatio
short: He desires to seek 'the land of foreigners' far from here; often read as the religious exile of the 'peregrinus'.
body: 'Elþeodig' is 'foreign, from another people'; 'eard' is 'land, homeland'. 'Monað modes lust' ('the desire of the mind urges') the spirit to travel. Dorothy Whitelock (1950) argued that the speaker is a 'peregrinus', a man who undertakes voluntary exile for the love of God, as Irish and Anglo-Saxon monks did. The 'land of foreigners' may be a literal destination or heaven, where all are strangers to earthly life. Earlier critics, beginning with Rieger, thought the poem a dialogue of an old sailor and a young man. Smithers (1957, 1959) argued for a figurative reading of the voyage. Most now read one speaker and a religious meaning, often allegorical.

title: No man so proud (ll. 39-43)
short: No man on earth is so proud, so generous, so bold or so favoured by his lord that he does not fear his sea-journey.
body: The passage uses the repeated 'to þæs' ('so') in a series: not so 'modwlonc' ('proud of mind'), nor so 'god' in gifts, so 'hwæt' ('bold') in youth, so 'deor' ('brave') in deeds, so favoured by his lord ('dryhten', which also means 'the Lord'). The ambiguity of 'dryhten' supports the allegorical reading: 'to hwon hine dryhten gedon wille' ('as to what the Lord will do with him').

anchor: Ne biþ him to hearpan hyge
title: No thought of harp or ring-giving
short: His mind is not on the harp, ring-giving, women or worldly hope, only on the rolling of waves.
body: 'Hringþegu' ('receiving of rings') is the gift from a lord. 'Wife wyn' ('pleasure in a woman'), 'worulde hyht' ('hope in the world'): the man who 'on lagu fundað' ('sets out on the sea') thinks only of 'yða gewealc' (as at l. 6). 'Longunge' ('longing') captures the restless desire that drives him. Critics read the passage as his renunciation of the worldly pleasures praised in heroic poetry.

title: Spring renewal (ll. 48-52)
short: Groves take on blossoms, towns grow fair, fields become beautiful, the world hastens on: all urge the eager mind to travel.
body: The spring passage contrasts with the winter of ll. 31-33. 'Byrig fægriað' means 'the towns grow fair'. 'Woruld onetteð' ('the world hastens on') suggests both spring's coming and the world's rush towards its end. Spring is the traditional season for voyages and for pilgrimages. Paradoxically, the beauty of the world makes the mind 'fus' ('eager, ready to depart', also used of the dying) for the journey. Some critics read the line as hinting at the end of the world.

title: The cuckoo, summer's guardian
short: The cuckoo urges with sad voice, 'summer's guardian', bodes sorrow bitter in the breast-hoard.
body: 'Geac' is the cuckoo, called 'sumeres weard' ('guardian, herald of summer'). In Old English poetry its call is sad: The Husband's Message (ll. 22-23) also has the cuckoo crying mournfully, as a signal to sail. In Celtic and Germanic tradition it can be a bird of sorrow. 'Breosthord' ('breast-hoard', the heart or mind) adds a container kenning. The cuckoo has sometimes been taken as the 'anfloga' of l. 62.

title: The mind leaves its enclosure
short: His mind now turns out of his breast-enclosure and travels wide over the whale's home, the earth's corners.
body: 'Hreþerloca' ('breast-locker') is a variant of The Wanderer's 'ferðloca'. Here the mind ('hyge', 'modsefa') goes out over the sea and comes back. 'Hwæles eþel' ('the whale's homeland') is a kenning for the sea, like 'hwælweg' (l. 63). Clemoes connected the passage to the patristic idea of the mind traveling while the body stays still ('mens absentia cogitans'). 'Eorþan sceatas' ('the corners of the earth') recurs at l. 105.

title: anfloga: the lone flier
short: The mind returns 'greedy and eager'; 'the lone flier' yells. What is the 'anfloga'? The cuckoo, a sea-bird, or the soul?
body: 'Anfloga' ('lone flier') occurs only here. Some take it as the cuckoo of l. 53, or another bird; others as the mind itself, which has been flying out and returns 'gifre ond grædig' ('greedy and eager'), and now cries. Several critics read the bird as the mind or soul in bird-form, an old image of the soul leaving the body. Clemoes related it to the mind's flight in Latin writing. 'Hweteð on hwælweg hreþer unwearnum' ('urges the heart irresistibly on the whale-way'). The crux is important for how one reads the poem's transition from voyage to eternity.

title: dryhtnes dreamas þonne þis deade lif
short: 'Hotter to me are the joys of the Lord than this dead life, transitory on land': the poem's turn to explicit faith.
body: 'Hatran' ('hotter', more ardent) recalls the hot cares of l. 11. 'Dream' means 'joy, festivity, music', and the 'dreamas' of heaven contrast with the 'deade lif' (the 'dead life'). 'Læne on londe' ('transitory on land') echoes The Wanderer's 'læne' litany. The word play on 'land' and 'sea' is significant: the land life is dead, while the sea voyage leads to heaven. Many critics see here the hinge of the poem.

title: adl oþþe yldo oþþe ecghete
short: One of three things always threatens: illness, age or the sword's hate takes away the life of the doomed.
body: 'Simle þreora sum' ('always one of three'), 'to tweon weorþeð' ('becomes a cause of doubt'). The three are 'adl' ('disease'), 'yldo' ('old age') and 'ecghete' ('edge-hate', violence of the sword). Beowulf has a similar list in Hroðgar's sermon (ll. 1763-68). 'Fægum fromweardum' ('the doomed one departing'): 'fæge' means 'fated to die'. The triad is a homiletic commonplace. Its use here makes the sea-voyage a figure for every human life, which must end in one of these ways.

title: lof lifgendra: fame turned heavenward
short: The best praise is to do good deeds against the devil, so that men praise one and one's fame lives among the angels.
body: 'Lof' ('praise, fame') is the heroic reward, the 'lastword' ('words after death'). Beowulf (ll. 1387-89) says a man should earn glory before death. The Seafarer redirects this ethic: deeds 'wið feonda niþ' ('against the malice of foes') and 'deofle togeanes' ('against the devil') will earn 'lof ... mid englum' ('fame among the angels'), 'ecan lifes blæd' ('the glory of eternal life'). Critics see here a deliberate Christian conversion of heroic fame.

title: cyningas ne caseras
short: There are no kings or emperors or gold-givers now as there once were: the world's glory is in decline.
body: 'Casere' is the Old English borrowing of Latin 'Caesar', 'emperor'. 'Dagas sind gewitene' ('the days are gone') and 'Gedroren is þeos duguð eal' ('this whole host has fallen'). The weaker ones remain and hold the world. 'Eorþan indryhto ealdað ond searað' ('the earth's nobility ages and withers'), as every man does. The decline of the world ('senectus mundi') and the comparison of the world's age to a man's age is from patristic tradition. The passage parallels The Wanderer's 'ubi sunt'.

title: flæschoma
short: The 'flesh-covering' or body can no longer swallow sweetness, feel pain, move a hand or think when life departs.
body: 'Flæschoma' ('flesh-covering', 'homa' = covering) is a common Old English poetic word for the body, the garment of the soul. When life ('feorg') is lost, the body cannot taste, feel, move or think. The theme of the body in death is common in Old English homilies and in the Soul and Body poems. 'Gomelfeax' ('grey-haired') describes the old man who mourns his friends 'eorþan forgiefene' ('given to the earth').

title: Gold in the grave (ll. 97-102)
short: Though a brother strew the grave with gold for his dead kinsman, gold cannot help the sinful soul before God.
body: The text is difficult: 'græf' is 'grave'; 'stregan' is 'strew'; 'byrgan be deadum' ('bury beside the dead'). Gordon and others discuss whether a brother is laying treasure in his brother's grave. The idea is close to Psalm 49:7 (KJV), 'None of them can by any means redeem his brother'. Gold buried for the dead, an echo of pagan burial rites, cannot help the soul 'for godes egsan' ('before God's terror'). The idea of treasure buried with the dead recurs in Beowulf.

title: The hypermetric homily (ll. 103-124)
short: The final section is gnomic and homiletic, partly hypermetric; many earlier editors thought it added and cut it.
body: 'Micel biþ se meotudes egsa' ('great is the terror of the Measurer'), 'forþon hi seo molde oncyrreð' ('before whom the earth turns aside'). Lines 103 and 106-108 are hypermetric, with longer half-lines. Some earlier editors and anthologists ended the poem at l. 108 or earlier and treated the rest as a later addition. Modern editors (Gordon, Klinck) keep the whole as one poem. Lines 109-116 are textually difficult, and editors punctuate and divide them differently. The ending has the gnomic 'Dol biþ ... Eadig bið ...' ('Foolish is he ... Blessed is he ...'), close to Maxims I.

title: Uton we hycgan hwær we ham agen
short: 'Let us consider where we have our home': the sermon-like close turns the exile's voyage into the journey to heaven.
body: 'Uton' ('let us') is a typical homiletic formula, used to exhort a congregation. The 'ham' ('home') is heaven, and the 'eadignesse' ('blessedness') that is reached 'in lufan dryhtnes' ('in the love of the Lord'). The poem closes with praise of the Lord and 'Amen', which suggests liturgical or homiletic use. This close completes the transformation of the sea-voyage into the voyage of life to heaven.
